Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "When the Bellweather College Film Society began planning its autumn series, its officers agreed that the screenings should feel less like a list of assignments and more like an invitation to spend an evening together. The society had about forty regular members, but the Thursday events were open to anyone on campus. First-year students often came because a friend had mentioned a film, while staff members from the library sometimes joined after work. The officers wanted to keep that informal welcome without losing the practical details that made each screening possible.

Mara Ellis, the society’s coordinator, reserved the small theater in the arts building for six Thursdays. She checked the dates against the college calendar and found that one evening overlapped with a campus theater rehearsal. Rather than move the whole series, she shifted that week’s screening to Wednesday and asked the theater manager to confirm the new time. The change also gave the society a chance to test a different projector before the busiest event of the term. Mara recorded the revised date on the society’s shared calendar and on the printed schedule beside the theater entrance.

The first film was a restored comedy from the 1930s, chosen by members at the spring meeting. The society’s treasurer, Imani Cole, found that the licensed copy included an introduction from a film historian, so the screening would run about fifteen minutes longer than the group had expected. Imani updated the event description and asked the café to keep its counter open until 9:30. The society did not promise refreshments; the café manager simply agreed that students could buy tea and sandwiches after the usual closing hour. That distinction mattered because the society’s modest budget covered room bookings and screening rights, not food.

1. The officers divided the remaining preparation into three jobs: checking the film files, arranging the room, and welcoming visitors. Leo, who managed the equipment cabinet, tested each file on the theater’s playback system rather than assuming that a successful laptop preview would be enough. Nia and Sam planned to set out chairs in two blocks, leaving a wide aisle for late arrivals and wheelchair users. Mara offered to greet guests at the entrance and explain that the society did not require membership or advance registration. They also agreed that one officer would remain near the doors during the introduction in case a visitor needed help finding a seat.

The society kept two email lists, and a small mistake in the first announcement prompted a careful discussion. One list was for members and volunteers; the other was for public event notices. The historian had supplied a personal address for arranging the introduction, but Mara did not add it to either list. In the internal planning thread, she wrote, “Please keep Dr. Vale off the volunteer list; he only needs the run time and the entrance instructions.” She sent him those two details in a separate message. The officers checked the recipients before sending the public notice, which included the time, location, film title, and a note about the longer introduction. No one treated the historian as a member of the society, and he was not copied on discussion of staffing or the budget.

On the afternoon of the screening, Leo discovered that the restored file had subtitles embedded in the image rather than supplied as a separate track. He watched several minutes in the theater and confirmed that the lettering remained readable from the back row. The discovery did not require a change to the program, but he told Mara so she could mention the subtitles in the introduction. Nia arrived early with a roll of paper signs and placed one at the arts building entrance, where visitors coming from the library would see it. Sam checked the aisle and moved a chair that had been left beside the accessible route.

Dr. Vale arrived shortly before the doors opened. Mara welcomed him and showed him the small table where he could leave his notes. He asked whether he should speak before or after the film, and she explained that the group had scheduled his introduction first so people could hear about the restoration without interrupting the screening. His remarks lasted seven minutes. He described how the restoration team had compared several surviving prints, and he pointed out a scene in which a change in lighting revealed a detail that earlier copies had obscured. The audience listened closely, then settled as Leo dimmed the house lights.

The screening began a few minutes after the posted time because a class had taken longer than expected to clear the theater. Mara apologized at the door to people who had been waiting, but she did not try to hurry the departing students. Once the film started, the audience stayed quiet, with scattered laughter at the physical comedy and a brief rustle when someone opened a paper wrapper. Afterward, several students asked Dr. Vale about the restoration process. One wanted to know whether the studio had intended the final scene to be ambiguous; another asked how the team had decided which print to use. Dr. Vale answered both questions and then left to catch a bus across campus.

At the next officers’ meeting, Imani reported that ticket donations totaled less than the society had collected at the previous year’s opening event, while attendance was slightly higher. The officers decided not to interpret either figure as a verdict on the series, since the earlier event had included a guest band and a larger room. They noted that the café had sold out of sandwiches but still had tea, and that several visitors had asked for the next screening date. Mara updated the public calendar with the Wednesday screening and added a reminder that the room would open fifteen minutes before the film. The society kept the historian’s address in its correspondence folder for future event arrangements, separate from both mailing lists.

The final screening of the series fell during the college’s reading period, so the officers chose a shorter documentary and booked an afternoon slot. That event drew fewer people, but two students who had first attended the opening comedy returned with classmates. After the room was cleared, Nia found a handwritten note on the welcome table thanking the society for making the screenings easy to attend. She passed it around at the next meeting, and the officers added a second entrance sign to their equipment checklist.
